title: Predicting Nanofabrication Variance: A Conditional Diffusion Model
authors: Wenhan Zhang, Ben Mills, Oleksandr Buchnev, Kevin F. MacDonald
abstract: Micro- and nanostructures fabricated by focused ion beam (FIB) milling invariably deviate from input designs due to systematic and stochastic effects such as ablation-rate fluctuations, and redeposition. As such, nominally identical iterations of a given process yield a distribution of non-identical fabrication outcomes, leading to variations in the physical (optical, mechanical) properties of fabricated structures. Existing models of the milling process typically predict a single deterministic fabrication result, neglecting this variability. Here we present a conditional diffusion model that learns the statistical distribution of process outcomes conditioned on input design, enabling it to predict a realistic distribution of possible output sample structures. These predictions accurately reproduce edge morphology, linewidth variations, and defect probabilities observed in fabricated samples, enabling statistical analysis of milling performance and the identification of dominant structural and process parameter-dependent deformation modes. The work establishes a probabilistic modelling framework for fabrication variability analysis and fabrication-aware design optimization.
summary: This paper introduces a conditional diffusion model to overcome the limitation of deterministic fabrication simulations by modeling the full statistical distribution of outcomes from FIB milling. By training on input masks and resulting SEM images, the model predicts an ensemble of possible structures, allowing for statistical analysis of process variability. This establishes a probabilistic framework for designing robust nanostructures.
main_problem: Existing models for nanofabrication processes, such as Focused Ion Beam (FIB) milling, predict only a single deterministic outcome, failing to account for the inherent stochastic variability caused by physical fluctuations.
main_result: The conditional diffusion model successfully predicts a realistic *distribution* of possible output sample structures, accurately capturing variations in edge morphology, linewidths, and defect probabilities observed experimentally.
method: The authors trained a conditional diffusion model, using a U-Net architecture and SPADE blocks, to learn the statistical distribution of fabricated outcomes conditioned on the input design mask.
model_or_system: The physical system is the fabrication of micro- and nanostructures (e.g., straight-line trenches) using FIB milling on thin gold films. The model learns the mapping from a binary input mask to the probability distribution of the resulting SEM image.
key_observables: Linewidth distributions, defect probabilities, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) modes characterizing structural deformation.
important_parameters: Ablation-rate fluctuations, redeposition effects, and the input design mask geometry.
main_assumptions: The model assumes that the statistical variability of the fabrication process can be effectively modeled by a conditional diffusion process, and that DDIM sampling provides sufficient fidelity for inference.
figures_summary: Figures compare simulated vs. experimental histograms of milled linewidths for straight-line trenches, and show PCA analysis comparing simulated and experimental structural deformation modes for complex geometries like split-rings.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of fabrication variability, details the conditional diffusion model training (forward/reverse process, loss functions), demonstrates its ability to generate an ensemble of realistic outcomes, and validates its predictions against experimental measurements of linewidths and structural modes.
why_interesting: While the physics is in materials science, the core methodology—using advanced generative ML models (Diffusion Models) to characterize the statistical uncertainty of a physical process—is highly relevant to modeling noise and uncertainty in quantum measurements or open quantum systems.
